content: Investing in well-integrated rabies elimination programs yields significant benefits. Every dollar spent not only contributes to the rapid reduction of human rabies deaths but also enhances access to healthcare for the most vulnerable populations globally. Rabies elimination serves as a model for One Health collaboration, requiring close cooperation between human and veterinary health sectors. This collaboration not only prevents human rabies but also establishes a framework for addressing other zoonotic diseases with pandemic potential. The One Health model is achievable even in lowand middle-income countries, where rabies disproportionately affects impoverished and rural communities. The economic burden of rabies, including losses in livestock and working animals, directly impacts resource-poor communities. Coordinated responses between animal and human health systems improve community livelihoods, strengthen disease surveillance, and enhance healthcare systems. In February 2015, the World Health Organization (WHO), the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE), and the Global Alliance for Rabies Control (GARC) launched the End Rabies Now campaign, aiming for zero human rabies deaths by 2030. This vision was endorsed globally in December 2015, aligning with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to end poverty and ensure universal health coverage. The WHO, OIE, and FAO have prioritized rabies elimination through global resolutions and commitments to reduce rural poverty and increase access to essential medicines. Rabies has plagued humanity for over 4,000 years, inspiring ineffective and often harmful remedies throughout history. In 1885, Louis Pasteur developed the first effective human rabies vaccine, marking a turning point in disease prevention. Modern vaccines and interventions have since eliminated dog-mediated human rabies in regions such as Western Europe, North America, Japan, South Korea, and parts of Latin America. Pilot programs in Africa and Asia have demonstrated the feasibility of rabies elimination, saving thousands of lives. In Latin America, coordinated efforts by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) have significantly reduced human rabies cases through mass dog vaccination campaigns, improved diagnostics, and public awareness initiatives. Between 1980 and 2010, laboratory-confirmed dog rabies cases decreased by 98%, and human rabies deaths declined by 97%. Similar successes have been achieved in countries like Mexico, South Africa, and Sri Lanka through community engagement, free access to post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), and robust surveillance systems. For the first time in history, the world is united in its goal to eliminate human rabies deaths by 2030. International health organizations, including WHO, FAO, OIE, and GARC, are collaborating to empower countries to implement rabies elimination programs. This global strategic plan integrates rabies prevention with other healthcare interventions, strengthening health systems and engaging stakeholders worldwide. The United Against Rabies collaboration provides a coordinated framework to support countries in developing and implementing national rabies elimination plans. By leveraging existing knowledge, tools, and technologies, countries can mobilize resources and political will to achieve their goals. Proven mechanisms, such as the Stepwise Approach towards Rabies Elimination (SARE), guide countries from initial data collection to sustained rabies elimination. Through harmonized global strategies and practical guidance, the United Against Rabies collaboration fosters capacity-building, advocacy, and resource mobilization. By prioritizing rabies elimination, countries can advance their SDG targets, improve public health, and save lives from this preventable disease. Rabies elimination is no longer a distant dream but a tangible goal supported by a united global effort.
